newsitem.title: CHINA: Foreign PCs fight to hold China market share.
newsitem.headline: Foreign PCs fight to hold China market share.

text.p: Foreign personal computer (PC) makers, grappling to maintain dominance in the fiercely competitive China market, are being forced to take aggressive defensive measures to hold market share, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Price is the key factor in the competition," the manager of one major distributor of foreign brand PCs in Shanghai said.
"The good performance of the domestic brands has pushed us to take more measures, including cutting prices to hold onto market share," he told Reuters.

The market share of most top foreign brand desktop PCs, including IBM, Compaq, AST and Digital, fell in the first half of 1997, figures from China Research Corp (CRC), an authoritative market surveyor, showed.

International Business Machines Corp's PC market share fell to 6.7 percent in the first half of this year from 7.9 percent in the year-ago period, according to the figures from CRC, a U.S. consultancy based in Beijing.
Compaq's share fell to 6.2 percent from 8.2 percent and AST Research Inc's share slipped to 3.8 percent from 7.9 percent, CRC figures showed.
The story was different for China's best-seller Legend, which during the same period saw solid sales growth to 133,360 PCs, grabbing a 10.4 percent market share from 8.0 percent in first half 1996.

"Domestic brand PC sales have rocketed over the past year and they are now estimated to have half of China's total PC market share with growth still above 50 percent," said a manager with a major distributor of IBM products.
"Foreign companies have lost a lot of ground, especially in the desktop segment, and they will lose more in the next few years," he said.
China sold 820,000 domestic brand PCs in the first six months of 1997, up 94.2 percent from the year-ago period, the Beijing-based Market Daily newspaper said on Wednesday.
China's personal computer market is expected to top three million units this year, up 50 percent on 1996, making it one of the world's most dynamic PC markets, official figures show.
Analysts said for notebook PCs, which use more advanced technology and occupy less than 20 percent of the total market, the dominant position of the top foreign brands was unshaken.
"Domestic firms still have no way to step into the laptop market, which is now shared almost totally by Toshiba, IBM and Taiwan's Twinhead," the manager said.
"Chinese PC companies are aggressively competing on price, and that is helping them win more and more customers from foreign companies," an industry analyst with a foreign consulting firm said.
Chinese brand prices were usually 30 percent to 40 percent cheaper than top foreign brands, analysts said.
The average price of a Chinese 586-class PCs, based mainly on Pentium and AMD (Advanced Micro Devices) chips, was around 10,000 yuan (1,205 US dollars), they said.
Many foreign PC companies had recently slashed prices in an effort to prevent further falls in their market share, analysts said.
Acer, one of Taiwan's major PC makers, in July announced a price cut of up to 20 percent on the China retail prices of its PCs, notebook and service computers.
IBM and Compaq also recently cut PC prices by around 10 percent to attract more local buyers, their distributors said.
